title: The Stock Market
description: Shares, prices, and why one company is a different bet from the whole market.
wolfLine: A price is the latest trade, not a promise.

ticker.definition: The short code a stock uses on an exchange, so you can find that company and not a different one.
ticker.example: A made-up company that trades as WOLF.

market-cap.definition: What the whole company is priced at: the share price times the number of shares.
market-cap.example: A $40 share and 2,000,000 shares is a market cap of $80,000,000.

price-to-earnings.definition: The share price divided by the company’s yearly earnings per share. It says how many dollars you pay for each dollar of those earnings. It is not a buy signal.
price-to-earnings.example: A $30 share with $2 of yearly earnings per share has a price-to-earnings of 15.

dividend-yield.definition: The yearly dividend divided by the share price, as a percent.
dividend-yield.example: A $1 yearly dividend on a $50 share is a 2% dividend yield.

lessons.title: What a Share Is
lessons.summary: One share is one piece, not the whole company.

steps.title: A piece, with a price
steps.body: A [[stock]] is a piece of a company. One share is one of those pieces. The price is what buyers and sellers agreed to most recently. It is not a promise of what the company is “really” worth.

steps.prompt: You buy 10 shares at $40. What do you own?
steps.explain: 10 shares are 10 pieces. The other shares belong to other owners.

steps.prompt: Those 10 shares cost $40 each. How many dollars did you pay?
The share price is a promise of what the company will be worth next year.
steps.explain: The price is the latest trade. Next year it can be higher or lower.

steps.prompt: A share of stock is closest to which idea?
choices: A savings account at a bank
steps.explain: Ownership. A [[bond]] is the loan. A share is a piece of the company.

lessons.title: Exchanges and Tickers
lessons.summary: The marketplace, and the short code.

steps.title: Where a share trades
steps.body: An exchange is the marketplace where shares are bought and sold. A [[ticker]] is the short code for one company on that marketplace. This course uses a made-up ticker, WOLF, so it is never a tip to buy a real company.

steps.prompt: What is a ticker?
choices: The short code that finds one company’s stock
steps.explain: The ticker is the code. The price and the dividend are different facts.

steps.prompt: What is an exchange?
choices: The marketplace where the shares trade
steps.explain: Buyers and sellers meet there. The latest trade sets the price you see.

steps.prompt: Two different companies can be the right one to buy just because their names look similar.
steps.explain: Names can be close. The ticker is how you check you have the company you meant.

steps.prompt: The short code for a stock is called its ___.
steps.explain: Ticker. Check it before you buy, so a similar name does not send you to the wrong company.

lessons.title: Why Prices Move
lessons.summary: A headline changes what people will pay.

story.title: The headline
story.body:
Nina owns **10** shares of a made-up company at **$40**, so **$400**. A news story says a big customer might leave.

Buyers will not pay $40 anymore. The price falls to **$32**.

steps.title: Meet Nina
steps.body:
Nina is 28 and a warehouse supervisor. She owns 10 shares of a made-up company, ticker WOLF, at $40. That is $400.

A news story says a big customer might leave. Buyers will not pay $40 anymore. The price falls to $32.

steps.prompt: Nina’s 10 shares fall from $40 to $32. How many dollars did she lose?
steps.explain: The drop is $8 a share. 10 × $8 = $80. Her $400 is now $320.

steps.prompt: What are the 10 shares worth at $32?
Why did the price fall?
choices: Buyers changed what they would pay after the news
steps.explain: The price is the latest agreement. Bad news can make that agreement a lower number.

steps.prompt: A falling price means Nina did something wrong.
steps.explain: Prices move because the crowd changes its mind. One owner cannot hold the old price in place.

steps.title: The whole price tag
steps.body: [[Market cap]] is the share price times the number of shares. A $40 price on a giant company is not “cheaper” than a $20 price on a tiny one. The whole price tag is the market cap.

steps.prompt: WOLF has 2,000,000 shares at $40. What is the market cap in dollars?
Company A is $20 a share. Company B is $40 a share. Which must be the bigger company?
choices: You cannot tell from the share price alone
Company A, because a low price means a giant
steps.explain: Share price is one share. Market cap is the whole company. You need the number of shares too.

steps.prompt: A $10 stock is automatically a better deal than a $100 stock.
steps.explain: The price is per share. A $10 stock can be a tiny company or a giant one with many shares.

steps.prompt: A company has a market cap of $80,000,000 and 2,000,000 shares. What is the price of one share?

lessons.title: Price and Earnings
lessons.summary: How many dollars for one dollar of earnings.

steps.title: A beginner ratio
steps.body: [[Price-to-earnings]] is the share price divided by the company’s yearly earnings per share. A result of 15 means you are paying $15 for each $1 of those earnings. It is a description, not a signal to buy or sell.

steps.prompt: A share costs $30 and the company earned $2 per share this year. What is the price-to-earnings?
steps.explain: $30 ÷ $2 = 15. You are paying $15 for each $1 of that year’s earnings.

steps.prompt: What does a price-to-earnings of 15 tell you by itself?
choices: That you should buy the stock
That you pay $15 for each $1 of those yearly earnings
steps.explain: It is a ratio. It is not a recommendation, and it does not remove risk.

steps.prompt: A low price-to-earnings guarantees the stock will rise.
steps.explain: Cheap on a ratio can still be a weak company. The ratio does not promise a return.

steps.prompt: You pay $15 for each $1 of yearly earnings. On $2 of earnings per share, what share price does that describe?

steps.title: Cash, as a percent of the price
steps.body: A [[dividend]] is cash some companies pay their owners. [[Dividend yield]] is that yearly cash divided by the share price. A $1 dividend on a $50 share is 2%. A high yield can also be a falling price, so it is not automatically good.

steps.prompt: A share pays a $1 dividend and costs $50. What is the dividend yield, in percent?
You own 20 of those $50 shares. How many dollars of dividends do you get in a year at $1 a share?
steps.explain: 20 × $1 = $20. The yield is still 2%.

steps.prompt: A dividend yield jumps from 2% to 6% because the share price fell and the dividend stayed $1. What happened?
choices: The price drop made the same $1 look bigger
The yield is a fee you pay
steps.explain: Yield is dividend ÷ price. A lower price raises the yield even when the cash did not change.

steps.prompt: Every stock pays a dividend.
steps.explain: Some companies pay none and keep the profits in the business. No dividend is not the same as a broken stock.

lessons.title: Reading a Quote
lessons.summary: Two numbers, and what they are not.

steps.title: The quote
steps.body: A quote is a snapshot. The last price is the latest trade. The dividend line is the cash the company pays in a year, if it pays one. Neither line is a prediction.

doc.title: Quote for WOLF
doc.subtitle: A made-up company, not a tip
doc.note: Dividend yield is the yearly dividend divided by the last price.

steps.prompt: What is the last price on this quote, in dollars?
steps.explain: The last price is $50. That is the latest trade, not a forecast.

doc.title: Quote for WOLF
doc.subtitle: A made-up company, not a tip
doc.note: Dividend yield is the yearly dividend divided by the last price.

steps.prompt: What is the dividend yield on this quote, in percent?
The last price on a quote is the price the company promises to buy the share back for.
steps.explain: It is the latest trade between buyers and sellers. The company is not promising that price.

steps.prompt: This quote is for a made-up ticker. Why does the course use one?
choices: So the lesson is a tip to buy a real company
So you can practice the numbers without a buy recommendation
Because real companies do not have tickers
steps.explain: WOLF is a teaching name. A real quote uses the same kind of lines, and this course still will not name a stock to buy.

lessons.title: One Stock or the Market
lessons.summary: A single headline can hit one company.

steps.title: The same dollars, two shapes
steps.body: Owning one [[stock]] means one company’s news is your news. A fund that holds hundreds of companies still rises and falls, but one failed product is a small piece of it. A later unit names that kind of fund. This lesson is only the contrast.

lines.label: A fund that owns hundreds of stocks

steps.prompt: A single bad headline hits one company. Which page takes the full hit?
steps.explain: The one-company page has nowhere else for the loss to hide. The fund still moves, but one company is a slice, not the whole $400.

steps.prompt: Both pages start at $400. The one stock falls 20%. How many dollars is that page worth?
steps.explain: $400 × 0.80 = $320. The whole page took the drop.

steps.prompt: A fund of hundreds of companies cannot lose money.
steps.explain: The whole market can fall. Spreading out avoids one company’s disaster. It does not avoid every drop.

steps.prompt: Why might a beginner use a broad fund instead of picking one company?
choices: Because one company’s bad year is not the whole account
steps.explain: The point of the many is that one failure is a piece. Nothing here is guaranteed.

lessons.title: Sharpen Up
lessons.summary: Smart repetition on what you’re closest to forgetting.

lessons.title: Den Trial: The Stock Market
lessons.summary: 8 questions. Three strikes and you’re out.

steps.prompt: You own 8 shares at $25. How many dollars did they cost?
A share pays $2 a year and costs $40. What is the dividend yield, in percent?
Market cap is the share price alone.
steps.explain: [[Market cap]] is the price times the number of shares.

steps.prompt: A price-to-earnings ratio is best read as what?
choices: A promise the price will rise
The dollars you pay per dollar of those earnings
steps.explain: It describes the price against earnings. It is not a buy signal.
